content: 1. In 2018, a study conducted in Geneva, Switzerland, focused on hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. The research emphasized decentralization, integration, and task-shifting in HCV testing and treatment, as analyzed through a global systematic review and meta-analysis published in The Lancet Global Health in 2021. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines in 2017 on hepatitis B and C testing, providing a framework for improving diagnostic and treatment strategies globally. 3. UNITAID published a report in 2019 titled Hepatitis C Diagnostic Technology Landscape, which outlined advancements in diagnostic tools for HCV. 4. Peeling et al. (2017) discussed the future of viral hepatitis testing, highlighting innovations in testing technologies and approaches in BMC Infectious Diseases. 5. Applegate et al. (2018) explored the challenges and advancements in HCV diagnosis, referring to it as the Holy Grail in Infectious Disease Clinics of North America. 6. WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services were published in 2015, emphasizing the importance of early diagnosis and linkage to care. 7. A systematic review by the WHO Global Health Impact Group Team in 2020 evaluated the clinical impact of point-of-care early infant diagnosis for HIV, underscoring its significance in improving health outcomes. 8. The WHO released recommendations in 2013 for the use of the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in diagnosing pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis in adults and children. 9. The PRISMA statement, published in BMJ in 2009, provided detailed guidelines for reporting systematic reviews and meta-analyses of studies evaluating healthcare interventions. 10. WHO prequalification of in vitro diagnostics in 2017 included the Xpert HCV Viral Load assay, which demonstrated its utility in diagnosing and monitoring HCV infection. 11. Draper et al. (2021) reported on the outcomes of the CT2 study in Yangon, Myanmar, which implemented a one-stop-shop model for community-based HCV testing and treatment, as published in Liver International. 12. McGrath et al. (2019) conducted a meta-analysis of median data using a one-sample aggregate approach, published in Statistics in Medicine. 13. Nyaga et al. (2014) introduced MetaProp, a Stata command for performing meta-analyses of binomial data, in Archives of Public Health. 14. Egger et al. (1997) identified bias in meta-analyses using a simple graphical test, as detailed in BMJ. 15. Higgins et al. (2003) developed a method for measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses, published in British Medical Journal. 16. Hoy et al. (2012) modified an existing tool to assess the risk of bias in prevalence studies, demonstrating interrater agreement in Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 17. Sterne et al. (2016) introduced ROBINS-I, a tool for assessing risk of bias in non-randomized studies of interventions, published in BMJ. 18. Le Roux and Odayar (2020) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the clinical and operational impact of point-of-care versus laboratory-based nucleic acid testing for routine HIV viral load monitoring. 19. The GRADE framework, as explained by Siemieniuk and Guyatt, provides a systematic approach to rating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations in clinical practice. 20. Sonderup (2021) described a simplified model of care for HCV treatment among people who inject drugs in Pretoria, South Africa, emphasizing accessibility and effectiveness. 21. Valencia et al. (2020) addressed the HCV care cascade in vulnerable populations with limited healthcare access in Madrid, Spain, using a point-of-care approach. 22. Saludes et al. (2020) evaluated the Xpert HCV VL Fingerstick point-of-care assay and dried blood spot HCV-RNA testing as simplified diagnostic strategies among people who inject drugs in Catalonia, Spain. 23. Martel-Laferriere et al. (2019) assessed the impact of single-day HCV investigations on treatment initiation among people who inject drugs in Quebec, Canada. 24. Japaridze et al. (2020) explored the decentralization of HCV testing to harm reduction sites in Georgia as part of the HEAD-START initiative. 25. Walker et al. (2020) analyzed the cost-effectiveness of a simplified treatment model using direct-acting antivirals for chronic HCV in Cambodia, published in Liver International. 26. Khalid et al. (2020) examined the HCV screening and diagnostic cascade in a primary healthcare clinic in Karachi, Pakistan, through a cohort study. 27. Mohamed et al. (2020) demonstrated the benefits of point-of-care screening and streamlined linkage to care in improving HCV treatment uptake among prisoners in England. 28. Ustianowski et al. (2020) reported on the success of a rapid test-and-treat program facilitating HCV micro-elimination in a women’s prison. 29. The London Joint Working Group on Substance Use and Hepatitis C piloted HCV testing in needle and syringe provision community pharmacies in 2018 and 2019. 30. Bajis et al. (2020) evaluated HCV testing, liver disease assessment, and treatment uptake among people who inject drugs in Australia before and after universal access to direct-acting antiviral treatment. 31. Zhang et al. (2021) assessed a decentralized HCV testing and treatment model integrated into the public health system in rural Cambodia, published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 32. Hamid et al. (2021) identified the lower age limit for HCV screening in large elimination programs in highly endemic areas, as discussed in The Lancet Gastroenterology. 33. Rewari (2020) highlighted community-based care models and testing strategies for HCV in high-burden areas in India, focusing on Uttar Pradesh. 34. Schürch et al. (2020) examined the management of HCV in opioid agonist therapy patients in Switzerland, published in Swiss Medical Weekly. 35. Davies et al. (2020) reported on the micro-elimination of HCV in a remand prison in Swansea, UK, as part of the EASL conference. 36. Mohamed et al. (2020) analyzed the cost-effectiveness of strategies to improve HCV screening, linkage-to-care, and treatment in remand prison settings in England. 37. Mafirakureva et al. (2021) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of HCV screening and treatment using direct-acting antivirals in a primary care setting in Karachi, Pakistan. 38. Agwuocha (2019) discussed expanding access to HCV viral load testing outside centralized settings in Nigeria. 39. Duchesne et al. (2020) provided model-based cost-effectiveness estimates of testing strategies for diagnosing HCV in Central and Western Africa, published in PLOS One. 40. Duchesne et al. (2020) also evaluated cost-effectiveness estimates of HCV testing strategies among people who inject drugs in Senegal, published in International Journal of Drug Policy. 41. WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis were updated in 2020, providing comprehensive recommendations for diagnosis and treatment. 42. WHO released updated recommendations in 2021 on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral initiation, and monitoring. 43. Markby et al. (2020) demonstrated the feasibility of innovative HCV testing and treatment models in Punjab and Delhi, India, as part of the HEAD-START project. 44. Remy et al. (2019) highlighted the use of real-time HCV viral load testing to increase outreach and linkage to care, published in Journal of Hepatology. 45. Thingnes et al. (2019) discussed challenges in delivering point-of-care HCV RNA testing in mobile health services for people who inject drugs. 46. Lazarus et al. (2020) described a novel HCV intervention in Denmark to test and treat people who inject drugs. 47. Shih et al. (2020) reported on a same-day test and treat model for chronic HCV and HBV infections in Egypt, published in Journal of Viral Hepatitis. 48. Llerena et al. (2020) explored micro-elimination strategies beyond prison walls, focusing on non-custodial sentences and telemedicine-assisted treatment. 49. WHO released a 2017 information note on the adoption and use of multi-disease testing devices in integrated laboratory networks. 50. The studies included in the review were geographically distributed across Africa, the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean, Europe, Southeast Asia, and the Western Pacific, as shown in the figures and tables summarizing study characteristics and outcomes.
